analysis.one_liner: Replaces asbestos lawsuits with a no-fault federal compensation fund paid for by asbestos companies and insurers.
analysis.headline: After the Senate agreed to take up the bill 98–1 and its committee approved it, a budget-rule objection killed it: a motion to set the rule aside won 58 votes but needed 60, and the bill was sent back to committee and never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: Asbestos has sickened hundreds of thousands of workers, and lawsuits over it have dragged through courts for decades and pushed many companies into bankruptcy. The FAIR Act would have shut down those lawsuits and replaced them with a national no-fault system: companies and insurers would pay roughly $90 billion into a federal fund, and sick workers would file claims there instead of in court, with fixed payment amounts by severity of illness. It would also have banned asbestos-containing products and funded mesothelioma research. The bill had broad bipartisan support, but it died on a Senate budget-rule vote rather than an up-or-down vote on its merits.
analysis.who_benefits: People diagnosed with asbestos-related diseases — shipyard and insulation workers, miners, and residents of places like Libby, Montana — would get guaranteed no-fault compensation without proving anyone was at fault, with fast-track payment for mesothelioma and the terminally ill. Companies facing asbestos lawsuits would gain an end to unpredictable jury verdicts in exchange for scheduled contributions. The trial bar would lose most of its asbestos docket.

how_it_helps.text: Claimants would not have to prove anyone was negligent; they would qualify based on medical diagnosis and evidence of exposure, on a no-fault basis [S3].
The Administrator would have to propose a decision on each claim within 90 days, and a complete claim with no decision within 180 days would be deemed accepted and paid [S3].
Claims by mesothelioma patients, people with less than a year to live, and families of those who died would be expedited and could be settled quickly [S4].
Asbestos companies would owe at least $3 billion a year for 30 years, totaling $90 billion, to guarantee the fund pays claims [S3].
The bill would fund medical screening and monitoring programs, ten mesothelioma research and treatment centers, and a national mesothelioma registry [S3].
It would ban the manufacture, processing, and distribution of asbestos-containing products, with limited exemptions [S3].
Workers and residents near Libby, Montana — the site of the worst vermiculite-asbestos contamination — would have exposure requirements waived and special claims procedures [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Asbestos defendant companies would pay scheduled contributions totaling $90 billion, and insurers would pay amounts set by a new Asbestos Insurers Commission. Claimants would pay in another way: they would give up jury trials and open-ended verdicts in exchange for fixed award amounts, reduced for prior recoveries and for smoking history, paid out over three years.

drawbacks.text: The fund would be the exclusive remedy: new and pending asbestos lawsuits would be barred in any court, so claimants would trade the right to a jury trial and potentially larger verdicts for fixed award amounts [S3].
Awards would be set by disease level, reduced for claimants who smoked, reduced for other compensation already received, and generally paid over three years rather than upfront [S3].

Companies that had already escaped asbestos liability through bankruptcy reorganization would be excluded from paying into the fund, shifting more of the burden onto those still exposed to suits [S4].
Attorneys representing claimants could receive no more than 5 percent of an award, sharply limiting legal representation for claimants compared with the contingency-fee system [S4].

The fund's solvency rested on the $90 billion defendant obligation with minimum $3 billion annual payments for 30 years, and the Administrator could reduce collections after the tenth year — raising the risk that money would run short and claims would go unpaid [S3].
Pending claims would be stayed (frozen) while the program started up, with a 24-month deadline after which claimants could return to court if the fund was not operating [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a real trade-off, not a giveaway in either direction. Sick workers would get faster, guaranteed money instead of years of litigation that many die before finishing, and a product ban and research funding would prevent future disease. The price was large: juries and open-ended verdicts would be replaced by a fixed schedule that in many cases pays less than a court award, smokers and prior claimants would see reductions, companies already shielded by bankruptcy would pay nothing, and whether $90 billion was enough was contested. Critics, including many Democrats and labor unions, argued the fund was underfunded and the defendant exemptions too broad; supporters argued certainty for both sides beat a broken court system. The Senate never got to settle that argument — the bill died on a budget-rule vote, not a vote on its merits.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate agreed nearly unanimously to take the bill up and debated it for days, but when a budget-rule objection was raised, the motion to set the rule aside got 58 of the 60 votes it needed, so under the Budget Act the bill was sent back to the Judiciary Committee and never came to a final vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced April 19, 2005 by Senator Specter with six original cosponsors and referred to the Judiciary Committee [S1].
The committee held hearings on April 26 and November 17, 2005, met in markup repeatedly, and reported the bill with amendments on June 16, 2005, placing it on the Senate calendar [S6].

On February 7, 2006, the Senate invoked cloture on the motion to proceed — the vote to begin debating the bill — by 98–1, with 44 of 44 Democrats, 53 of 55 Republicans, and the Independent in favor [S7].
The Senate debated the bill February 8–14, 2006; committee amendments were withdrawn, and a point of order under the Congressional Budget Act was raised against the measure [S6].

On February 14, 2006, the motion to waive the Budget Act failed 58–41, short of the 60 votes needed: 44 of 55 Republicans and 13 of 44 Democrats voted to waive, while 30 Democrats and 11 Republicans voted no [S8].

With the waiver rejected, the bill was recommitted to the Judiciary Committee under the Budget Act, its cloture motion was withdrawn, and it never received a final vote before the 109th Congress ended [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos defendant companies avoided a $90 billion funding obligation and continued defending claims case by case, while asbestos victims kept their right to jury trials and potentially larger verdicts — but also kept the delays and bankruptcies of the court system. Labor unions and trial lawyers who argued the fund was inadequate succeeded in stopping it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asbestos companies avoided paying; claimants kept lawsuits

sides.party_line_note: The vote to begin debate was 98–1, but the decisive vote split mostly by party: 44 of 55 Republicans and 13 of 44 Democrats voted to waive the budget rule, while 30 Democrats and 11 Republicans voted no.

industries.note: The bill would have capped their total liability at $90 billion, ended asbestos lawsuits against them, and stopped litigation-driven bankruptcies — but required scheduled contributions to fund victims' compensation. Their gain in certainty came partly at claimants' cost, since fixed awards replaced open-ended jury verdicts.

They would have had to pay into the fund in amounts set by a new Asbestos Insurers Commission, but in exchange their open-ended asbestos exposure would have ended and contract adjustments were specified [S3].

Making the fund the exclusive remedy would have wiped out most asbestos court cases and capped attorney fees at 5 percent of awards, though claimants also would have gained a faster, guaranteed payment system [S3,S4].

industries.industry: Asbestos product manufacturers, including the chlor-alkali industry
industries.note: Title V would have banned manufacture and distribution of asbestos-containing products; the chlor-alkali industry and encapsulated roofing products won specific exemptions from the ban [S3].

The bill would have incorporated existing bankruptcy trusts into the new fund and credited their payments against defendant obligations, absorbing a system built through chapter 11 reorganizations [S3,S4].
